title: Human Sacrifice in Iron Age Britain: The Ones Thrown Into Storage Pits Were Outsiders
dek: The five sets of human bones from the storage pits at the Duropolis site in Dorset are not like the bog bodies: these were not venerated elites but malnourished, hard-labouring outsiders with their wrists bound.
why: Archaeologist Miles Russell uses first-hand material from 17 years of excavation to strip ‘human sacrifice’ back from Roman propaganda to testable skeletal evidence. Dense with information, but it demands a little patience.
who: Listeners interested in Iron Age archaeology, the credibility of Roman texts, prehistoric religion and ritual violence; anyone who wants to see how archaeology reasons back from bones to social structure.
skip: The first 2 minutes of small talk and T-shirt chatter can be skipped; the mid-episode Gone Medieval ad can be skipped outright.

points.h: Romans condemned human sacrifice while watching gladiators
points.body: Roman writers described the Britons as savages who practised human sacrifice, ate people and married their sisters, and Caesar's wicker man is part of that propaganda. But Miles points to a double standard: the Romans thought killing to please a god was wrong, yet they crucified thousands and let gladiators be torn apart by wild beasts in the arena as public entertainment. The difference is not whether you kill but who the killing is for — killing for a god is barbaric, killing for an audience is enforcement. That cultural blind spot is the starting point for understanding every Roman account of human sacrifice.

points.h: Ninety-nine percent of Britons never entered the burial record
points.body: To judge whether there was human sacrifice, you first need bones. But in most of late Iron Age Britain there is almost no skeletal remains at all, and Miles estimates that roughly 99% of the population never appears in the archaeological record — they may have been cremated, left exposed, or thrown into rivers or bogs. Only a few regions, such as Dorset and East Yorkshire, have large inhumation cemeteries. That means ‘no evidence of human sacrifice found’ and ‘no human sacrifice’ are two different things: the silence of archaeology is itself a sampling problem, not a conclusion.

points.h: Lindow Man was killed by four methods stacked together
points.body: Lindow Man is England's most famous bog body, with the upper body beautifully preserved: neatly trimmed nails, groomed hair, good nutrition, suggesting he was well treated in life. But he died what Miles calls a ‘fourfold death’ — a blow to the head that fractured the skull, a cut throat, strangulation, and finally being placed face down in the bog possibly still alive, with water found in his lungs. The cut throat plus strangulation was to make the blood spray further, a theatrical execution. In his stomach were an oatcake and mistletoe, the latter possibly used to induce hallucinations or dull pain, bringing him closer to the divine.

points.h: The bones in storage pits were not buried, they were discarded
points.body: At hillforts such as Danebury, human bones often turn up at the bottom of disused cylindrical storage pits, mixed in with animal bones. Some are just a skull with the mandible and a few cervical vertebrae, indicating death by decapitation rather than removal of the head after death; others were thrown in whole. Miles stresses that this is not a formal burial, with relatives laying the body down in tears and grave goods, but ‘someone being disposed of in a very dramatic, violent way’. Yet bones in pits could also be heroes who fell in battle, so bones alone cannot distinguish execution, death in combat and human sacrifice — the key is whether the burial context is anomalous.

points.h: Winterbourne Woman had her throat cut and was thrown onto a bone platform
points.body: In 2010 an adult woman was found at the bottom of a storage pit at Duropolis, face down on a layer of long-weathered horse, cattle and pig bone. Her skeleton showed a blow to the chest a few weeks before death, a cracked rib that was healing, and head trauma, but the fatal injury was a deep cut on the cervical vertebrae — someone had opened her carotid artery from behind with a blade. DNA showed she was unrelated to any of the families in the cemetery, isotopes showed she did not grow up on the chalk, and severe compression of her vertebrae indicated long-term load-bearing. Miles concludes she was probably a slave or prisoner of war, an ‘outsider’, and that is why she was chosen.

points.h: This society was matrilocal, so they did not kill their own
points.body: DNA research by Laura Cassidy and University College Dublin shows that at Duropolis women stayed on the same land for generations while men came from further away and were more weakly linked to the women, that women had more grave goods, and that land may have passed down the female line. This explains a brutal logic: the people thrown into the pits were not local women, because they were the landholders and possibly the spiritual leaders who presided over rituals. Miles says that looking at their roundhouses and settlements you would think it a utopia, but seeing the human sacrifice makes you realise their attitude to life was completely different from ours.

points.h: At the pit edge the archaeologist sees a crime scene
points.body: Five probable human sacrifices have been found at Duropolis: four clearly thrown in, with limbs scattered; one face down but with the legs folded under the body, possibly having been bound. One adult male had one leg against the pit wall and his foot in the topmost layer, so the archaeologists dug down to the foot before reaching the man and could clearly reconstruct how he was thrown in from the pit mouth after being killed. Miles says that normally you excavate people who were buried, but this time ‘you're actually dealing with a murder victim’ — you can see the victim, the method of death and the place of death, but you will never find the killer.

points.h: The bog holds elites, the pits hold the bottom of society
points.body: Miles proposes a stratified theory: bog bodies such as Lindow Man and the Irish examples have clean nails and no calluses on their hands, did no heavy labour, and may have been priests or ruling elites, with some scholars even arguing they were kings — power traded against ‘ultimately sacrificing yourself’. The people in the Duropolis storage pits did heavy work, were malnourished and had their wrists bound, belonged to the bottom of society, and were seen as more expendable. Both are human lives given up, but the bog is ‘claimed by the gods’, while the storage pit is merely ‘thrown in with the rubbish’.

terms.def: An ancient human body preserved in acidic, oxygen-poor peat bog, where skin, internal organs and even stomach contents can survive.
A transitional zone between two worlds, such as rivers and bogs, believed to be inhabited by gods and to offer passage to another world.
A social form in which men move after marriage to live with the woman's family, with land and status often passing down the female line.
Inferring an individual's place of growth, diet and migration from the ratios of isotopes in bones and teeth.
A fungus parasitic on grain that can cause hallucinations, speculated by some scholars to have been used before sacrifices to alter the sacrificial victim's state of consciousness.
